strengths: The paper provides a coherent theoretical framework (Definition 1, Propositions 1-4) linking module 'plasticity' (average Lipschitz-type rate of change) to finetuning behavior, with full proofs in the appendix.

Extensive empirical validation: plasticity is measured across 11 benchmarks, two model scales (ViT-Base 86M, ViT-Huge 632M), and the empirical ranking (MHA > FC1 > FC2 > LN2 > LN1) is highly consistent with theory across nearly all settings shown in the extensive appendix figures.
The finetuning study is large-scale and careful (~800 runs, multiple learning rates, 3 seeds per configuration), and robustness/statistical testing (Wilcoxon signed-rank) is reported.

The connection drawn between input-output Lipschitz continuity and gradient norms during optimization is a clear, testable mechanistic story, and the gradient-norm/validation-loss trends in the appendix consistently support the narrative.
The related work and limitations sections are thorough and honest, and the paper is clearly written with good figures summarizing the pipeline (Fig. 2).
weaknesses: Significant confound: MHA/FC1/FC2 each have ~28M trainable parameters while LN1/LN2 have only ~18K (Table 3). The reported performance gap could largely be attributable to trainable capacity rather than 'plasticity' per se; the paper does not control for parameter count (e.g., comparing plastic vs equally-sized less-plastic subsets, or normalizing by parameter count) to isolate the causal effect claimed.

The practical effect sizes are small: full-finetuning baseline (90.9%) is on par with or only marginally better than MHA-only tuning (90.8%), and the decrease between MHA and FC1 is only 0.07% (not statistically significant per Table 1), undermining the strength of the 'components to prioritize' recommendation beyond what is already known (MHA/FFN > LayerNorm), which is consistent with prior empirical findings (e.g., Touvron et al. 2022; Ye et al. 2023) that this paper mainly re-confirms rather than substantially extends.

The theoretical upper bounds (Proposition 3/4) are acknowledged to be extremely loose (orders of magnitude, ~10^6) relative to observed plasticity values, so the 'theory' mainly provides a qualitative ranking rather than quantitatively predictive bounds; the paper leans on this qualitative ranking as its central theoretical contribution.

No new adaptation method is proposed; the paper is purely observational/analytical, with the combination with reparameterization methods (e.g., LoRA on plastic components) left as future work, limiting immediate practical impact.

Some theoretical assumptions (e.g., identical per-position mean/std across tokens for the LayerNorm bound, bounded-energy image assumption) are somewhat strong and not empirically verified, though the paper argues informally for their plausibility.

The component-wise 'in isolation' study, while methodologically clean, does not test realistic combinations (e.g., MHA+FFN jointly vs. LayerNorm-only), which is closer to how PEFT methods are used in practice, limiting the direct actionability of the guidance.

strengths: The paper is very thorough empirically: ~800 finetuning runs across 11 classification benchmarks, 2 model scales (ViT-Base, ViT-Huge), multiple seeds and learning rates, with full implementation and reproducibility details provided in the appendix.
The theoretical development (Propositions 1-4) is carefully proved and gives a principled, if loose, derivation of upper bounds on the plasticity of LayerNorm, feedforward, and attention modules.

The writing is clear, the figures are informative, and the narrative connecting plasticity to gradient norms during optimization (via Béthune et al. 2024) is intuitive and consistently illustrated (Fig. 1, Fig. 4).
The appendix analysis of gradient norms and validation loss trajectories across all benchmarks/seeds/learning rates is a nice level of diligence that supports the internal consistency of the story.
weaknesses: Critical confound: the five finetuning configurations differ drastically in number of trainable parameters (MHA/FC1/FC2 each ~28M, 33% of the model, vs LN1/LN2 at only 18K, 0.02%, as shown in Table 3/Table 4). The entire empirical 'benefit of plasticity' story could simply be a capacity/parameter-count effect rather than a smoothness/plasticity effect, and the paper never controls for this (e.g., no experiment comparing plasticity-matched components with similar parameter budgets, or parameter-matched subsets of attention/FFN vs normalization).

The practical effect sizes are small and partly non-significant: Table 1 shows the average performance decrease of FC1 relative to MHA is only 0.07% (not statistically significant), and even FC2 is 0.44%; only the comparison to LayerNorms (0.8-0.9%) reaches significance. This undermines the strength of the central claim that plasticity ranking predicts finetuning benefit in a strong, actionable way.

The theoretical ranking derived in Section 4 does not fully match the empirical ranking (FC1 vs FC2, LN1 vs LN2 ordering has to be 'refined' empirically), weakening the claim that the theory provides principled a priori guidance; in practice the theory mainly separates attention/FFN from LayerNorms, a distinction already well established via parameter count intuition.

The attention upper bound in Proposition 3/4 is many orders of magnitude looser than the other bounds (Fig. 6, up to 10^6 larger), which the authors attribute to looseness of attention Lipschitz estimation rather than a genuine qualitative difference; this raises doubts about whether the theoretical ranking is meaningfully informative versus an artifact of bound tightness.

The main actionable takeaway (prioritize attention and FFN layers over LayerNorm during selective finetuning) is not new and is already demonstrated empirically in prior work cited by the authors themselves (Touvron et al. 2022; Ye et al. 2023); the paper's novelty rests almost entirely on the post-hoc theoretical/plasticity explanation rather than a new, more effective finetuning strategy or method.

No downstream demonstration that the plasticity perspective yields a new, better PEFT method (e.g., applying LoRA selectively to high-plasticity components, as suggested in future work, is never actually tried), leaving the practical significance of the framework largely conceptual.

The connection between input-output Lipschitz/plasticity and the weight-gradient norms relied upon for the optimization argument is motivated qualitatively via a cited result (Béthune et al., 2024) rather than established rigorously in this paper's specific setting, so the causal mechanism remains more suggestive than proven.

strengths: Clear, well-motivated research question bridging empirical PEFT practice and theoretical understanding of transformer component adaptability

Rigorous theoretical contribution: correctly derived, non-trivial upper bounds on plasticity for LayerNorm, feedforward, and multi-head attention, including a tightened attention bound via an image-energy argument
Strong alignment between theory and experiments: the theoretical plasticity ranking (MHA > FC1 > FC2 > LN2 > LN1) is validated across ViT-Base and ViT-Huge and across sequence lengths

Extensive, robust experimental validation: ~800 finetuning runs across 11 diverse benchmarks (standard, corrupted, domain-shifted), multiple learning rates, and 3 seeds, with statistical significance testing
Mechanistic explanation connecting plasticity to gradient norm magnitude and optimization dynamics, consistently illustrated across many additional figures in the appendix
Thorough, transparent appendix with full proofs and implementation details supporting reproducibility
Honest discussion of limitations and promising directions (LLMs, adaptive optimization, combination with reparameterization methods like LoRA)
weaknesses: Large magnitude gap between theoretical upper bounds and empirical plasticity values (orders of magnitude), indicating the bounds are loose and mainly useful for qualitative ranking rather than quantitative prediction
Modest effect sizes in finetuning performance gains (e.g., ~0.07-0.9% average accuracy differences between MHA and other components), tempering the practical significance of the central claim
Study restricted to single-component finetuning in isolation; it remains unclear how the plasticity ranking translates to realistic PEFT setups that combine multiple components simultaneously
Claimed extension of theoretical insights to LLMs/transformer decoders is argued but not empirically tested in this paper

Experiments limited to one pretraining regime (ImageNet-21k supervised pretraining) and one architecture family (ViT), leaving generality to other pretraining paradigms (e.g., self-supervised) unverified

The LayerNorm plasticity bound relies on a simplifying assumption (identical token statistics across inputs at each position) whose practical tightness is asserted rather than thoroughly empirically verified

strengths: Introduces a well-motivated and somewhat counter-intuitive perspective connecting component-level smoothness/Lipschitz properties ('plasticity') to finetuning performance, explicitly contrasting with the common assumption that smoothness aids adaptation.

Solid theoretical contribution: derives rigorous upper bounds on the plasticity of LayerNorm, feedforward layers, and multi-head self-attention (including a tighter bound using an image-energy argument), with full proofs provided in the appendix.

Very extensive empirical validation: plasticity measured across 11 diverse classification benchmarks, three ViT scales (86M/307M/632M), and extended to DINOv3 and GPT-2, consistently confirming the theoretical ranking MHA > FC1 > FC2 > LN2 > LN1.

Large-scale finetuning study (~1000 runs) with both SGD and Adam, multiple learning rates and seeds, plus a low-data VTAB-style regime, showing a consistent and statistically tested (Wilcoxon) relationship between plasticity and finetuning accuracy/stability.
Good mechanistic story linking plasticity to gradient norm magnitude and loss descent speed during optimization (Fig. 1, 5), which is empirically verified rather than just asserted.
Strong attention to reproducibility: released code, detailed hyperparameters/preprocessing, and carbon footprint reporting.
Interesting practical byproducts, e.g., single-component (LayerNorm) finetuning with Adam outperforming LoRA with far fewer parameters, showing parameter count alone doesn't determine adaptability.
weaknesses: The theoretical upper bounds are extremely loose for the attention module (orders of magnitude larger than empirically observed plasticity, acknowledged in Appendix E.1.1), so the theoretical 'ranking' argument is essentially qualitative/heuristic rather than a tight, predictive quantitative result; the actual ordering is established mainly by direct empirical measurement.

The finetuning experiments only tune one component type at a time (isolated), which is a somewhat artificial setting relative to how PEFT is typically used in practice (combining multiple module types, e.g., attention + norms, or LoRA across several projections); it is unclear how well the 'prioritize high-plasticity components' recommendation generalizes to joint/combined tuning scenarios.

Confounding between plasticity and parameter count is not fully disentangled: MHA/FFN have ~28M trainable parameters vs. ~18K for LayerNorms, so higher capacity alone could partly explain better finetuning performance; while the paper offers one LoRA comparison to argue against a pure parameter-count explanation, a more direct controlled ablation (e.g., comparably-sized non-smooth vs. smooth modules) would strengthen the causal claim.

Reported accuracy gains from prioritizing MHA over LayerNorms are numerically modest in many settings (roughly 1 accuracy point on average across 11 benchmarks), so while statistically significant, the practical significance for real deployment decisions is not fully established.

The finding that attention benefits most from finetuning partially overlaps with prior empirical results (e.g., Touvron et al. 2022), somewhat tempering the novelty of the practical takeaway, even though the theoretical framing (plasticity) is new.

The plasticity metric itself (average rate of change over pretraining vs. downstream image pairs) is a proxy quantity whose direct causal link to finetuning benefit (beyond correlating with gradient norms, which is separately and more directly shown) could be discussed more critically.

strengths: Very extensive empirical campaign (~1000 finetuning runs, 11 benchmarks, multiple model scales up to 632M parameters, SGD and Adam, low-data VTAB regime) that consistently supports the central empirical observation that attention/FFN finetuning outperforms LayerNorm-only finetuning.

Clean theoretical derivations (Propositions 1-4) bounding the average rate of change ('plasticity') of each component type, with full proofs in the appendix, extending prior Lipschitz-attention results (Castin et al., 2024) to a new quantity.

Plasticity ranking is shown to be consistent not only across ViT scales but also across a self-supervised ViT (DINOv3) and a decoder-only LM (GPT2), suggesting the measured phenomenon (rate of change by component type) is somewhat architecture-general.

Strong reproducibility practices: open-sourced code, detailed hyperparameter tables, carbon footprint reporting, and a large appendix of consistency checks (per-dataset plasticity plots, per-seed training curves).

The gradient-norm/validation-loss analysis (Fig. 5 and appendix) provides a plausible mechanistic link between plasticity and optimization dynamics, which is a nice qualitative narrative tying theory to practice.
weaknesses: Severe confound between 'plasticity' and trainable parameter count: MHA/FC1/FC2 have ~28M trainable parameters each versus ~18K for LN1/LN2 (Table 5). The central empirical claim that 'high plasticity leads to better finetuning' is equally, and more parsimoniously, explained by capacity differences rather than smoothness/plasticity per se. The paper never isolates these two factors (e.g., by finetuning a subset of attention/FFN weights matched in parameter count to LayerNorm, or inflating LayerNorm's effective capacity) so the causal story is not convincingly established.

The LoRA comparison (Section 5.2, 'A strong baseline') showing LayerNorm+Adam beats LoRA with fewer parameters on one dataset (Cifar100) is a single anecdote and does not resolve the capacity confound for the paper's main claims across 11 benchmarks.

The theoretical upper bounds (Propositions 3-4) are acknowledged by the authors themselves to be extremely loose in practice (orders of magnitude larger than the empirically measured plasticity, up to 10^6-10^8 vs. single-digit/low-double-digit empirical values in Fig. 7 vs Fig. 3), which weakens the claim that the theory is doing meaningful predictive work beyond qualitative ordering; the 'theoretical ranking' is essentially confirmed post hoc by the empirical measurements rather than by a tight, falsifiable bound.

The connection between plasticity (a forward-pass input-output sensitivity measure on the pretrained, frozen model before finetuning) and the actual finetuning dynamics (which involve weight updates throughout training) relies on a fairly informal argument (citing Béthune et al., 2024, Thm 1) rather than a direct theoretical treatment of the specific finetuning setting studied; the empirical gradient-norm correlation (Fig. 5) is suggestive but not a rigorous causal demonstration.

Novelty of the core empirical finding is limited: that tuning attention (and to a lesser extent FFN) outperforms tuning only normalization layers during selective finetuning has already been observed in prior work (e.g., Touvron et al., 2022; Lee et al., 2023), which the paper itself cites as 'reminiscent.' The main contribution is thus primarily a new explanatory lens (plasticity) rather than a new finding, and that lens is undermined by the capacity confound above.

Benchmarks used for the finetuning study are relatively small/simple (CIFAR variants, DomainNet, Flowers, Pets); it remains unclear whether the plasticity-performance relationship would hold on larger-scale, more realistic finetuning tasks or for LLMs, which are only studied at the level of static plasticity measurement (not actual finetuning benefit).

Within the paper's own statistical testing, FC1 is not significantly different from MHA (Table 1), slightly undercutting the cleanliness of the proposed strict ranking (MHA → FC1 → FC2 → LN2 → LN1) as a practical guideline.

strengths: Comprehensive theoretical analysis (Propositions 1-4) deriving plasticity upper bounds for each ViT component with full proofs, including a tightened attention bound using an image-energy argument.

Extensive empirical validation across ViT-Base/Large/Huge, DINOv3 (self-supervised), and GPT2 (decoder-only LM), and 11 diverse classification benchmarks, showing a consistent plasticity ranking (MHA > FC1 > FC2 > LN2 > LN1).
Large-scale finetuning study (~1000 runs) across multiple learning rates, 3 seeds, SGD and Adam optimizers, and a low-data (VTAB) regime, with statistical significance testing (Wilcoxon signed-rank).
Coherent mechanistic narrative connecting plasticity to gradient norm magnitude and loss descent speed during optimization, illustrated clearly in Figures 1 and 5.
Strong reproducibility support: open-source code, detailed hyperparameters, carbon footprint reporting, and extensive appendix figures for every benchmark/seed combination.
Practically relevant byproduct showing single-component finetuning (e.g., LayerNorm or MHA alone) can rival or beat parameter-heavy PEFT methods like LoRA.
weaknesses: Large gap (several orders of magnitude) between theoretical upper bounds and empirically observed plasticity for the attention module, limiting the quantitative (as opposed to qualitative/ordinal) predictive value of the bounds.
Components are only finetuned in isolation; no experiments combine multiple high-plasticity modules (e.g., MHA+FC1), which is more representative of common PEFT practice.

Absolute accuracy differences between configurations, while statistically significant, are sometimes modest, and the paper could better contextualize practical significance relative to parameter/compute cost.

No finetuning experiments on LLMs/decoder-only models despite claiming the theory extends there; this remains purely a plasticity-analysis extension, leaving the main practical claims unvalidated for text domains.

Comparisons between components with vastly different parameter counts (e.g., MHA vs LayerNorm) are not normalized by parameter count or FLOPs in the main results, which could affect practical interpretation of which component to 'prioritize' under a fixed budget.
